Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

The Mercantile Registry (Registro Mercantil) for the province of the company's registered office, under the Directorate-General for Legal Security and Public Faith (Dirección General de Seguridad Jurídica y Fe Pública). Incorporation deeds are authorized by a Spanish notary.

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July, approving the consolidated text of the Spanish Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital), particularly Articles 4, 20, 21, 22, 23, 31, 32, 33, 40, 210, and 233; Royal Decree 1784/1996 on the Mercantile Registry; and Law 14/2013 on support for entrepreneurs, as amended.

Formation / constitutional filings

Public deed of incorporation (escritura pública de constitución), filed for registration with the competent provincial Mercantile Registry.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 66 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

An SL may be formed with share capital of EUR 1 or more. Capital contributions must be fully subscribed and paid at incorporation. While capital is below EUR 3,000, statutory safeguards apply: at least 20% of annual profit must be allocated to legal reserve until capital plus reserve reaches EUR 3,000, and, on liquidation with insufficient assets, shareholders may be jointly liable for the shortfall up to EUR 3,000. No general statutory escrow account is required. Non-cash contributions require a description and valuation in the deed; founder liability rules apply.

Funding & unlock path: Comply with applicable municipal fire-prevention and building approvals, the Spanish Building Code, workplace risk-prevention requirements under Law 31/1995, and applicable industrial-safety regulations. Fire-service review or certification, structural/load checks, and commissioning inspections depend on the premises, equipment, and regional/local rules. Obtain any required construction, occupancy, activity, and industrial-facility approvals before use.

Paid-in capital rule: An SL may be formed with share capital of EUR 1 or more. Capital contributions must be fully subscribed and paid at incorporation. While capital is below EUR 3,000, statutory safeguards apply: at least 20% of annual profit must be allocated to legal reserve until capital plus reserve reaches EUR 3,000, and, on liquidation with insufficient assets, shareholders may be jointly liable for the shortfall up to EUR 3,000. No general statutory escrow account is required. Non-cash contributions require a description and valuation in the deed; founder liability rules apply.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
RESOLVED, that the Company accepts the subscriptions and payments for the shares set out in the incorporation deed and confirms that the subscribed capital has been fully paid. RESOLVED, that the registered office be established at [full address], Spain, subject to registration and any required premises approvals. RESOLVED, that [name] is appointed [sole director/joint director], and [name] is appointed [secretary/other officer, if applicable], with the powers and term provided in the bylaws and applicable law. RESOLVED, that the director is authorized to obtain the Company’s tax identification number, complete registration and tax filings, open bank accounts, and apply for required activity, industrial, environmental, and product-compliance authorizations.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Mandatory Environmental Clearance

No single national industrial licensing board applies. The competent authority is the autonomous community’s industrial-safety department for industrial-facility registration and applicable product-market surveillance, together with the municipality for premises and activity approvals. AESA (Agencia Estatal de Seguridad Aérea) regulates relevant UAS operations, not general drone manufacture.

Category: No single Spain-wide manufacturing operating permit title. Depending on the site and process, the required authorization may be a municipal activity or environmental license, or a responsible declaration, together with registration of applicable industrial facilities in the autonomous community. Determine the exact instrument from the facility location, processes, capacity, and emissions.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) – Central Electronic Portal: sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

A non-resident foreign entity engaged in taxable operations in Spain must obtain a Spanish Tax Identification Number (NIF) for legal persons, format N + 8 digits. The procedure is: (1) appoint a tax representative if the entity is not established in the EU/EEA and no reciprocity exemption applies; (2) execute a power of attorney in favour of the representative or legal counsel; (3) file Form 036 (Declaración censal) electronically through the AEAT portal or by paper at the competent local tax office, accompanied by certified incorporation documents, the foreign tax identification certificate or VAT registration evidence, and the appointment of the Spanish representative where required; (4) receive the provisional NIF, subject to validation; (5) after AEAT verification, obtain the definitive NIF and, if making taxable supplies, the Spanish VAT registration number. Entities established in the EU may instead use the VIES exchange mechanism and are registered under their EU VAT ID plus the Spanish intra-EEA operator code where applicable.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A non-resident foreign entity engaged in taxable operations in Spain must obtain a Spanish Tax Identification Number (NIF) for legal persons, format N + 8 digits. The procedure is: (1) appoint a tax representative if the entity is not established in the EU/EEA and no reciprocity exemption applies; (2) execute a power of attorney in favour of the representative or legal counsel; (3) file Form 036 (Declaración censal) electronically through the AEAT portal or by paper at the competent local tax office, accompanied by certified incorporation documents, the foreign tax identification certificate or VAT registration evidence, and the appointment of the Spanish representative where required; (4) receive the provisional NIF, subject to validation; (5) after AEAT verification, obtain the definitive NIF and, if making taxable supplies, the Spanish VAT registration number. Entities established in the EU may instead use the VIES exchange mechanism and are registered under their EU VAT ID plus the Spanish intra-EEA operator code where applicable.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain does not operate a US-style check-the-box regime; an Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) is a per-se corporation taxable at entity level under Impuesto sobre Sociedades. Available elective mechanisms relevant to the tax profile include: (a) the elective consolidation regime for groups of companies under Article 58 et seq. of Ley 27/2014 (at least 75% direct or indirect ownership for 1 year); (b) the reduced 15% corporate income tax rate for newly created SLs engaged in an economic activity during the first two taxable years if the entity opts for that special regime and meets the filing conditions; (c) intercompany allocation and Spanish permanent establishment closing agreements; (d) no hybrid or anti-hybrid 'elections' are available—ATAD transposition rules (Articles 15 bis through 15 nonies Ley 27/2014) apply mandatorily to deny mismatches.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

There is no general turnover-based registration threshold for established businesses; any entrepreneur or professional carrying out taxable supplies is required to register and become a taxable person from the first transaction. For non-established EU vendors making distance sales of goods into Spain, the applicable EU-wide annual distance-selling threshold is EUR 10,000, above which Spanish VAT becomes due and SPAIN VAT registration is required. Non-EU foreign vendors have no registration threshold and must register from the first taxable supply in Spain, subject to reverse charge mechanisms on certain B2B supplies.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods to non-EU destinations qualify for 0% VAT under Article 21 of the Spanish VAT Law when the goods are physically dispatched or transported out of the EU by the seller, by the customer, or on behalf of either party, and the seller has in its possession within the statutory timeframe an accepted customs export declaration (DUA) evidencing departure from EU customs territory. For supplies related to agricultural drone equipment, the same zero-rating applies provided the drones are actually shipped outside the EU; installation, commissioning, remote support and related offshore services supplied to a non-EU business customer are generally zero-rated or outside the scope of Spanish VAT if the reverse charge applies, subject to the place-of-supply rules. The exporter must retain transport documents, payment evidence and the customs exit confirmation (passed to the 'E-AD' or CMR / B/L / AWB records) to demonstrate the principal condition: the goods left Spain within 90 days of dispatch.

  • Customs Export Declaration (DUA – Documento Único Administrativo) showing the accepted 'Salida de la UE' customs status
  • Export accompanying document (EAD) or customs warehouse release confirmation
  • Bill of Lading, Air Waybill, CMR or equivalent transport document proving physical departure from EU territory
  • Commercial invoice issued by the exporting SL
  • Packing list and, where relevant, certificate of origin or movement certificate EUR.1
  • Bank SWIFT / TT wire credit or Inward Remittance Certificate evidencing receipt of export consideration
  • Payment guarantee or letter of credit instruments if payment is deferred, plus correspondence evidencing the payment schedule

Spain imposes phased mandatory B2B electronic invoicing under Ley 18/2022 ('Crea y Crece'), requiring interoperable electronic invoices in structured format for all commercial transactions between private businesses once the implementing regulation is fully effective. In parallel, the AEAT real-time system 'Suministro Inmediato de Información' (SII) applies to large taxpayers with annual invoicing above EUR 6,000,000 and to entities in certain regimes, requiring transmission of invoice records to AEAT's web services/API within 4 days of invoicing. The Verifactu regime under Ley Antifraude (Ley 11/2021) obliges all billing software to produce authentic, complete, integral, legible and traceable invoice records ('Registro de Facturación') and to make those records electronically available to AEAT upon request. There is no separate mandatory digital stamp or pre-clearance of individual invoices for the standard SL exporter, but the combination of SII, Verifactu and upcoming Crea y Crece interoperability constitutes the real-time clearance framework.

Export zero-rating claims are subject to strict AEAT audit scrutiny. Acceptance of a DUA with subsequent non-departure, fictitious exports, manipulated transport documents, or failure to produce credible proof of dispatch within the 90-day rule will trigger adjustment of the zero-rated supply to 21% VAT, with late-payment interest and input VAT clawback. Under Ley 58/2003 General Tributaria, an incorrect application of the zero rate is a taxable 'regularisation' attracting surcharges (recargos del periodo ejecutivo) of 5% to 20%, and in cases of negligence or intent, proportional penalties of 50% to 150% of the amount. False documentation supporting an export claim may be treated as tax fraud, carrying potential criminal liability under the Spanish Criminal Code and, where customs value or export licenses for dual-use or security-sensitive goods are involved, sanctions under Spanish customs and export-control law. Forensic cross-checks through the AEAT computer systems, maritime manifest databases, and banking payment records are routine; failure to receive export proceeds within the 180-day documentary benchmark increases the presumption of artificiality and invites retrospective clawback.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain is a full convertibility jurisdiction under the euro area legal framework. Both current account transactions (goods, services, royalties, dividends, profit remittances) and capital account movements are generally unrestricted under Articles 63–66 TFEU and Spanish Act 19/2003 on Foreign Investment. The euro is freely convertible; there are no domestic exchange controls, quantitative limits, or prior administrative FX licensing requirements. Profit and dividend remittance to non-residents is permitted without exchange-control authorization, but is subject to substantive tax requirements including the non-resident income tax withholding (currently 19% for outbound dividends, plus possible treaty relief) and Bank of Spain statistical reporting. A strategic foreign-investment screening regime under Law 7/2020 and Royal Decree 571/2020 applies to non-EU/EFTA investors acquiring Spanish targets in critical sectors (dual-use, critical technologies, security, strategically sensitive physical or digital infrastructure). For an AgTech drone sprayer with ISIC 2821 production and potential dual-use UAV classification, the screening threshold should be assessed at the very early stage: if non-EEA ownership exceeds the statutory thresholds (10% or direct control, or 5% in regulated strategic areas), prior authorization may be required; otherwise, an ex-post declaration to the Foreign Investment Registry suffices. Capital reparations and inward equity investments require no central bank permit, but the funds must reach a Spanish bank account and be reported through the balance-of-payments declaration framework.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Under EU law and Spanish legislation there is no mandatory export-proceeds surrender ratio, no forced conversion timeline, and no requirement that export receipts be repatriated to Spain within a fixed period. The exporting SL may retain hard-currency proceeds in resident accounts, use them directly for foreign debt service or inputs, or convert them to EUR at freely negotiated bank rates. However, intermediaries must report all cross-border transactions to the Banco de España balance-of-payments statistics in accordance with Bank of Spain Circular 4/2004, with individualized reporting for transactions equal to or exceeding EUR 50,000 (or the prevailing updated threshold). For documentary compliance, the exporter must maintain the customs export declaration (DUA), the commercial invoice, transport documents (airway bill, bill of lading), and, for UAV-related products, the relevant dual-use/export-control end-user certificate or authorization under EU Regulation 2021/821. The statutory no-surrender treatment does not exempt the SL from providing full supporting evidence to the receiving bank upon conversion of foreign currency into EUR, nor does it waive tax documentation for export income.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España — Central Bank of Spain, operating within the European System of Central Banks; external financial affairs and foreign-investment oversight also involve the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Digital Transformation and the Commercial and Foreign Investment Registry under the Secretary General for Investment and Foreign Trade

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Feasibility rating: Medium for a well-regulated EEA-licensed EMI that can operate in Spain under PSD2 passporting, and Low for non-EEA offshore EMIs. A Spanish SL can maintain a virtual IBAN, receive trade payments, and settle operational costs through an EMI, provided the EMI holds a valid payment institution licence under Directive (EU) 2015/2366 and is registered in Spain through the Bank of Spain passport register. However, offshore digital EMIs (e.g., chartered in a non-EEA jurisdiction without an EU branch) are not permitted to hold Spanish-resident local nostro accounts or issue Spanish IBANs unless they establish a locally authorized branch or agent bank. The main legal constraints are: AML obligations under Act 10/2010, the prohibition on unlicensed payment activity, the need for segregated client accounts, and the practical reluctance of tier-1 Spanish banks to accept an offshore EMI as a counterparty for high-value AgTech export settlements. In consequence, the preferred route is to open a primary treasury account at a tier-1 Spanish bank and use an EEA-licensed EMI only for collection of payments from overseas B2B customers or disbursement of small trade expenses.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Industry classification as manufacturing of unmanned aerial systems (UAS/drones) with dual-use and export-control implications

Root cause: Industry classification as manufacturing of unmanned aerial systems (UAS/drones) with dual-use and export-control implications

Defense evidence: Comprehensive documentation package: (1) EU Dual-Use Regulation 2021/821 effective authorization or written exemption confirmation from the Spanish Secretary of State for Trade; (2) product specification sheets evidencing the non-weaponisable agricultural spraying design, spraying flow rates, battery capacity, and military-spec limitation strategies; (3) end-user certificate from each agtech customer; (4) corporate export-control manual with internal compliance program, screening logs, and denial-list checks; (5) copy of the SL's ISO 9001 quality or CE/ENAC certifications; (6) independent trade counsel legal opinion classifying the product as EAR99/ITAR-free comparable dual-use low-tier if relevant; (7) patents and utility model filings showing agritech purpose.
Complex or non-EU Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) structure, including trust, offshore holding, or non-resident shareholders in the drone manufacturing entity

Root cause: Complex or non-EU Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) structure, including trust, offshore holding, or non-resident shareholders in the drone manufacturing entity

Defense evidence: Dossier containing notarized and apostilled incorporation deed (escritura pública) of the Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada; current Registro Mercantil certificate; completed UBO register filing (RDL 7/2021 and EU Directive 2015/849) with passport and tax residence certificate of each UBO; full corporate chain chart from legal counsel; statutory balance sheet and bank reference detail; sworn declarations of source of wealth and source of funds; third-party compliance due-diligence report; certification that no politically exposed person (PEP) is involved or, if so, a PEP declaration and enhanced-compliance plan.
Planned inbound capital injection from non-EU jurisdiction exceeding EUR 250,000 without a previous banking relationship

Root cause: Planned inbound capital injection from non-EU jurisdiction exceeding EUR 250,000 without a previous banking relationship

Defense evidence: The SL must provide: (a) signed investment or shareholders agreement covering the capital increase; (b) notarized board resolution approving the injection; (c) source-of-funds evidence such as audited financial statements of the investor for the last three years, bank account statements for the preceding twelve months, and tax-residence certificate of the investing entity; (d) confirmation of the origin of wealth from the remitting bank; (e) a sworn certificate from the accounting auditor tracing this specific injection to declared corporate profits or documented asset disposal; (f) foreign investment registry filing confirmation (ex-post declaration path); (g) escrow agreement signed with the receiving Spanish bank to ensure traceability of funds from the source bank account to the SL's corporate capital account.
Payments through high-risk jurisdictions or trade counterparties involving agrochemical inputs or agricultural customers without robust sanctions screening

Root cause: Payments through high-risk jurisdictions or trade counterparties involving agrochemical inputs or agricultural customers without robust sanctions screening

Defense evidence: Evidence bundle comprising: commercial invoices and contracts with final beneficial flow; customs export/import declarations; phytosanitary certificates for agricultural inputs; safety data sheets for any agrochemical substances; OFAC and EU Consolidated List screening result reports generated by a reputable compliance database; an end-user certificate from each counterparty; transport documents including bill of lading or airway bill with full cargo description; corporate cross-border payment policy demonstrating compliance with international sanctions; written certification that payments will not involve U-turn transactions or trans-shipment to sanctioned entities; and a duty-of-care report under the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.
Use of a non-EEA or offshore digital EMI for collection of export proceeds, triggering heightened correspondent banking risk

Root cause: Use of a non-EEA or offshore digital EMI for collection of export proceeds, triggering heightened correspondent banking risk

Defense evidence: Defense package: copy of the EMI's payment institution licence or digital-bank charter from its home regulator; proof of Spain passporting/agent registration under PSD2; EMT/EMI audited financial statement for the previous year; client-money segregation confirmation from an independent auditor; monthly reconciliation of all receipts and outgoing payments to the governing Spanish treasury account; board-approved treasury policy stating that the EMI is a secondary collection channel only; Spanish-counsel legal opinion on the EMI's capacity to hold funds and the enforceability of customer agreements; and AML/KYC data-sharing agreement in compliance with GDPR and Act 10/2010.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Compliant wire transfer protocol for inbound capital injection into the SL: (1) Before transfer, the SL opens a EUR-denominated Capital Escrow Account at a tier-1 Spanish bank and executes an escrow agreement confirming the intended use (equity subscription or capital contribution). (2) The foreign investor instructs its bank to send an SWIFT MT103 using the SL's IBAN and the payment reference 'CAPITAL INCREASE' and Spanish balance-of-payments purpose code '601 – Inward direct investment' or '603' for non-resident capital contributions; field 70 must contain the investment registration number where applicable. (3) The sending bank must transmit the underlying investment agreement and evidence of regulatory/screening clearance if the investor is non-EU/EEA, to enable automatic credit via the correspondent account at the receiving Spanish bank. (4) The Spanish bank will verify the source of funds, conduct UBO and sanctions screening, and release the amount into the operational account after the notary deed of capital increase is filed at the Registro Mercantil. (5) The SL must submit the corresponding post-closing foreign-investment declaration to the Foreign Investment Registry of the Ministry of Economy within the statutory filing window (typically one month after execution); no prior central-bank FX permit is required for euro transfers. (6) All fees should be charged to the sending side using 'OUR' billing to preserve traceability and avoid reduction in the reported capital amount. If the capital is in USD or a non-euro currency, a sub-account or a treasury conversion arrangement with a recognized bank must be used, and the resulting EUR amount must match the corporate records.The primary clearing rails for outbound trade disbursements are: (a) SEPA Credit Transfer (SCT) for EUR payments to EEA suppliers, utilities, and European sub-distributors; (b) SWIFT MT103 direct telegraphic-transfer for immediate TT settlement in USD, GBP, or other convertible currencies, using the correspondent network of the Spanish bank; and (c) Commercial Documentary Letters of Credit (MT700/MT710) for large AgTech drone export contracts, with the SL as beneficiary and a Spanish bank as advising/confirming bank to mitigate non-payment and country risk. For USD disbursements to Latin American counterparties, the bank routes via US Fedwire/CHIPS through a New York correspondent; for transactions with China-related suppliers, the SL may use a standard MT103 with CNY offshore settlement (CNH) or the Commercial LC denominated in CNY, provided the bank has CNY clearing capabilities. The SL must include the correct ISO 20022 purpose code on each disbursement—typically 'TRDC' for trade, 'PDPE' for payment employment? or more practically the Spanish purpose code '010' for export/import trade settlements—and must attach pro-forma invoices, contracts, customs declarations, and the applicable export/import license. For cash management, the SL should operate an EUR operational account as the master treasury account and one USD or multi-currency settlement account; any excess FX exposure is systematically hedged through the treasury policy rather than left open. Incoterms and documentary requirements should match the settlement rail chosen, with a preference for LC payment terms on orders above a EUR 250,000 threshold.EUR/USD and EUR/GBP outright foreign exchange forward contracts (plain vanilla, flexible and window forwards) transacted with a Spanish credit institution under ISDA/EMTA documentationEUR/foreign-currency FX swap transactions for short-term liquidity management and rollover of export receivablesCross-currency interest-rate swaps (CCIRS) to hedge the currency and interest-rate risk of the initial capital injection or long-term foreign-currency debtNon-deliverable forward (NDF) contracts involving non-convertible or restricted currencies (e.g., Argentine peso, offshore CNY) executed through the Spanish bank's international NDF desk, subject to internal limit approvalOver-the-counter EUR/USD and EUR/Latin-American-currency collar structures (zero-cost collars, participating forwards) to cap hedging cost while retaining partial currency upsideExchange-traded futures options and currency futures on Eurex or CME, permitted under the SL's investment-policy threshold when the counterparty clearing exposure is within the treasury risk mandateFX options and exotic forward-based structures (accumulators/deccumulators) only where pre-approved by the bank's risk committee and the SL's board as part of a documented treasury hedging policyRisk participation agreements and trade finance interest-rate/currency facilities embedded in commercial export credit arrangements, authorized under Spanish banking regulations if the SL maintains qualified-investor status for the trade amount

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Feasibility rating: Medium for a well-regulated EEA-licensed EMI that can operate in Spain under PSD2 passporting, and Low for non-EEA offshore EMIs. A Spanish SL can maintain a virtual IBAN, receive trade payments, and settle operational costs through an EMI, provided the EMI holds a valid payment institution licence under Directive (EU) 2015/2366 and is registered in Spain through the Bank of Spain passport register. However, offshore digital EMIs (e.g., chartered in a non-EEA jurisdiction without an EU branch) are not permitted to hold Spanish-resident local nostro accounts or issue Spanish IBANs unless they establish a locally authorized branch or agent bank. The main legal constraints are: AML obligations under Act 10/2010, the prohibition on unlicensed payment activity, the need for segregated client accounts, and the practical reluctance of tier-1 Spanish banks to accept an offshore EMI as a counterparty for high-value AgTech export settlements. In consequence, the preferred route is to open a primary treasury account at a tier-1 Spanish bank and use an EEA-licensed EMI only for collection of payments from overseas B2B customers or disbursement of small trade expenses.
